## Question 1

Given $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x-6}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x+6}=\dfrac{3}{11}$, what is the value of $x$? &nbsp;&nbsp;
**A** $2\sqrt{15}$ &nbsp; **B** $4\sqrt5$ &nbsp; **C** $5\sqrt2$ &nbsp; **D** $\sqrt{58}$ &nbsp; **E** $50$
&nbsp; **F** $58$ &nbsp; **G** $60$ &nbsp; **H** $80$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer H
**H.**

**Step 1 — Combine the fractions.** With a common denominator,
$$\frac{1}{\sqrt x-6}-\frac{1}{\sqrt x+6}=\frac{(\sqrt x+6)-(\sqrt x-6)}{(\sqrt x-6)(\sqrt x+6)}=\frac{12}{x-36},$$
using $(\sqrt x-6)(\sqrt x+6)=x-36$.

**Step 2 — Solve.**
$$\frac{12}{x-36}=\frac{3}{11}\ \Rightarrow\ 12\cdot 11=3(x-36)\ \Rightarrow\ 132=3x-108\ \Rightarrow\ x=80.$$
*The surds vanish because the denominators are a difference of squares — always try that first.*
:::

## Question 2

Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{9}^{16}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt x}+\sqrt x\right)^{2}\mathrm dx-\int_{9}^{16}
\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt x}-\sqrt x\right)^{2}\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp; **A** 0 &nbsp; **B** 2 &nbsp; **C** 4
&nbsp; **D** 7 &nbsp; **E** 14 &nbsp; **F** 28 &nbsp; **G** 75 &nbsp; **H** 175

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer F
**F.**

**Step 1 — Use $(a+b)^2-(a-b)^2=4ab$.** With $a=\tfrac1{\sqrt x}$ and $b=\sqrt x$,
$$\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt x}+\sqrt x\right)^{2}-\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt x}-\sqrt x\right)^{2}=4\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt x}
\cdot\sqrt x=4.$$

**Step 2 — Integrate the constant.**
$$\int_{9}^{16}4\,\mathrm dx=4(16-9)=28.$$
*Never expand the squares — the identity turns the whole thing into a one-line constant integral.*
:::

## Question 3

Claim: for all positive reals $x,y$, $\sqrt{x^{y}}=x^{\sqrt y}$. Which is/are a counterexample? &nbsp;&nbsp;
**I** $x=1,y=16$ &nbsp; **II** $x=2,y=8$ &nbsp; **III** $x=3,y=4$ &nbsp;&nbsp; (options **A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer C

[*(Prf1 · counterexample — S5)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C** (II only).

**Step 1 — Rewrite both sides.** $\sqrt{x^{y}}=x^{y/2}$, so the claim is $x^{y/2}=x^{\sqrt y}$. For $x\neq1$
this holds only when $\tfrac y2=\sqrt y$, i.e. $y=4$; and for $x=1$ both sides are $1$.

**Step 2 — Test each.** A counterexample needs the two sides **unequal**.

- **I** ($x=1$): both sides $=1$ — equal, not a counterexample.
- **II** ($x=2,y=8$): $2^{8/2}=2^{4}=16$ but $2^{\sqrt8}\approx 7.1$ — **unequal**, a counterexample.
- **III** ($x=3,y=4$): $3^{4/2}=9$ and $3^{\sqrt4}=3^{2}=9$ — equal ($y=4$), not a counterexample.

So only **II**.
:::

## Question 4

A student's attempt to answer *"the largest number of consecutive odd integers that are all prime"* runs
I–VII (see paper) and concludes the answer is two. Best description? &nbsp;&nbsp; **A** correct … **H** first
error line VII.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer G

[*(Err — spot the error — S7)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G** (first error line VI).

**Step 1 — Check the claim.** $3,5,7$ are three consecutive odd integers, all prime, so the answer "two"
is wrong — the attempt is incorrect.

**Step 2 — Find the first error.** Lines I–V are all correct (one of any three consecutive odd integers is
a multiple of $3$). Line **VI** says "one of the integers is a multiple of $3$, **so not prime**" — but the
multiple of $3$ can be $3$ **itself**, which **is** prime (as in $3,5,7$). That unjustified "so not prime"
is the first error.
:::

## Question 5

$R$: $k$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$. &nbsp; $S$: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{k}\sin 2x\,\mathrm dx=0$. Which
is true? &nbsp;&nbsp; **A** necessary and sufficient &nbsp; **B** necessary, not sufficient &nbsp;
**C** sufficient, not necessary &nbsp; **D** neither

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer A

[*(Arg2 · necessary & sufficient — S3)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.**

**Step 1 — Do the integral.**
$$\int_{0}^{k}\sin 2x\,\mathrm dx=\left[-\tfrac12\cos 2x\right]_{0}^{k}=\frac{1-\cos 2k}{2}.$$

**Step 2 — Solve $S$.** $\dfrac{1-\cos 2k}{2}=0\Rightarrow\cos 2k=1\Rightarrow 2k=2n\pi\Rightarrow k=n\pi$
— exactly "$k$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$".

**Conclusion.** $S\Leftrightarrow R$, so $R$ is **necessary and sufficient** for $S$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

## Question 6

For $a>1$, $(*)$: $a^{x}=x$. Which equations must have the **same number of real solutions** as $(*)$?
&nbsp;&nbsp; **I** $\log_a x=x$ &nbsp; **II** $a^{2x}=x^{2}$ &nbsp; **III** $a^{2x}=2x$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
(options **A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer F
**F** (I and III).

**I — same equation in disguise.** $\log_a x=x\Rightarrow x=a^{x}$ (exponentiate). That is exactly $(*)$,
so the solutions are identical. ✓

**III — a substitution.** Put $u=2x$; then $a^{2x}=2x$ becomes $a^{u}=u$, which is $(*)$ in $u$. Since
$u=2x$ is a one-to-one relabelling, the number of solutions is unchanged. ✓

**II — an extra root sneaks in.** $a^{2x}=x^{2}$ means $(a^{x})^{2}=x^{2}$, i.e. $a^{x}=\lvert x\rvert$
(as $a^{x}>0$). For $x\geq0$ this is $(*)$; but for $x<0$ it also asks $a^{x}=-x$, and since $a^{x}\to0$
while $-x\to+\infty$, there is always **one more** solution with $x<0$. So II has more solutions. ✗

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-4,4,400); a=1.3
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.4))
plt.plot(x,a**x,label='y = a^x  (a=1.3)',color='#2b6cb0')
plt.plot(x,x,label='y = x',color='#dd6b20')
plt.plot(x,-x,'--',label='y = −x (the extra branch in II)',color='crimson')
plt.ylim(-1,5); plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.6); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title('II asks a^x = |x|, adding a solution where a^x meets −x (x<0)')
plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 7

The line $ax+by=c$ ($a,b,c\neq0$). Which is **necessary but not sufficient** for a positive gradient
**and** a positive $y$-intercept? &nbsp;&nbsp; **A**–**D** (sign conditions) &nbsp; **E** $a$ and $c$ have
opposite signs &nbsp; **F** $a$ and $c$ have the same sign

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer E

[*(Arg2 + coordinate geometry — S3)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**E.**

**Step 1 — Translate the two requirements.** In the form $y=-\tfrac ab x+\tfrac cb$, the gradient is
$-\tfrac ab$ and the $y$-intercept is $\tfrac cb$. We need
$$-\tfrac ab>0\ \ (\text{so }\tfrac ab<0)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \tfrac cb>0.$$

**Step 2 — Extract a sign relation.** From $\tfrac ab<0$ and $\tfrac cb>0$, dividing gives
$\tfrac{a}{c}<0$, so **$a$ and $c$ have opposite signs** — this is *necessary*.

**Step 3 — Why not sufficient.** Opposite signs of $a,c$ fix $\tfrac ac$ but say nothing about the sign of
$b$, so they do not guarantee both original conditions. Hence **necessary but not sufficient**.
:::

## Question 8

A (non-right) triangle. Count the straight lines dividing it into two triangles, **at least one**
right-angled. Can the student draw one with exactly **1** (I), exactly **2** (II), exactly **3** (III) such
lines? &nbsp;&nbsp; (options **A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer D
**D** (III only). In fact **every** non-right triangle has **exactly three** such lines.

**Step 1 — What a dividing line is.** To cut a triangle into two triangles the line must run from a
**vertex to a point on the opposite side** (a *cevian*). Any other cut leaves a quadrilateral.

**Step 2 — When a cevian makes a right-angled piece.** The right angle can only be
(i) at the foot on the opposite side — that forces the cevian to be an **altitude**; or
(ii) at the vertex it starts from — possible only if that vertex angle exceeds $90^\circ$.
(A base angle stays as the original acute angle, so it can't become the right angle.)

**Step 3 — Count.**

- **Acute triangle:** all three altitude feet lie inside the opposite sides, so the **three altitudes** each
  split it into two right triangles — and no vertex exceeds $90^\circ$, so nothing else. **Exactly 3.**
- **Obtuse triangle:** only the altitude from the obtuse vertex has its foot inside the opposite side
  (1 line); and the obtuse vertex admits **two** cevians making a right angle there (one perpendicular to
  each side). **Again exactly 3.**

So the count is always $3$: statement III holds, and **1 or 2 is impossible**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
A=np.array([0,0]); B=np.array([4,0]); C=np.array([1.3,2.6])   # acute triangle
def foot(P,Q,R):  # foot of perpendicular from R onto line PQ
    d=Q-P; t=np.dot(R-P,d)/np.dot(d,d); return P+t*d
plt.figure(figsize=(4.4,3.4))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0')
for P,Q,R,nm in [(B,C,A,'A'),(A,C,B,'B'),(A,B,C,'C')]:
    F=foot(P,Q,R); plt.plot([R[0],F[0]],[R[1],F[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1)
for P,nm in [(A,'A'),(B,'B'),(C,'C')]:
    plt.annotate(nm,P,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,4))
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('Acute triangle: the 3 altitudes are the 3 dividing lines',fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

:::

## Question 9

Pentagon $P$. $(*)$: *if at least one interior angle is $108^\circ$, then all the interior angles form an
arithmetic sequence.* Which are true? &nbsp;&nbsp; **I** $(*)$ &nbsp; **II** the contrapositive of $(*)$
&nbsp; **III** the converse of $(*)$ &nbsp;&nbsp; (options **A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer D

[*(Arg1 · converse & contrapositive — S2)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D** (III only).

**Step 1 — $(*)$ and its contrapositive are FALSE.** A pentagon can have one angle $108^\circ$ without the
angles forming an arithmetic sequence — e.g. $108^\circ,100^\circ,100^\circ,116^\circ,116^\circ$ (sum
$540^\circ$). So $(*)$ is false, and its **contrapositive** (always equivalent) is false too. That kills I
and II together.

**Step 2 — The converse is TRUE.** Converse: *if the angles form an arithmetic sequence, then one is
$108^\circ$.* A $5$-term arithmetic sequence has sum $5\times(\text{middle term})$, and the interior angles
of a pentagon sum to $540^\circ$, so the **middle** term is $540/5=108^\circ$. Hence one angle is always
$108^\circ$. **III is true.**

*Key: I and II share a truth value (equivalent), so any answer with exactly one of them — like III only —
must have both false.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

:::

## Question 10

An attempt to solve $x^{4}-2x^{2}-3<0$ by completing the square (lines I–VI, see paper). Which is true?
&nbsp;&nbsp; **A** completely correct &nbsp; **B**–**G** first error in line I–VI

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer A

[*(Err — spot the error — S7)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A** — the argument is completely correct.

**Step 1 — Check each "if and only if".** I adds $4$ to both sides; II writes $x^{4}-2x^{2}+1=(x^{2}-1)^2$;
III is $\lvert x^{2}-1\rvert<2$, i.e. $-2<x^{2}-1<2$.

**Step 2 — The one that looks suspicious (III→IV).** IV keeps only $x^{2}-1<2$ and drops "$-2<x^{2}-1$".
That is legal here because $x^{2}-1\geq-1>-2$ **always**, so the dropped half is automatically true — the
lines stay equivalent.

**Step 3 — Finish.** V is $x^{2}<3$; VI is $-\sqrt3<x<\sqrt3$. And indeed
$x^{4}-2x^{2}-3=(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}+1)<0\Leftrightarrow x^{2}<3$. Every step holds, so **A**.

*Not every "spot the error" question has an error.*
:::

## Question 11

Theorem $(*)$: *if $2^{k}+1$ is prime, then $k$ is a power of $2$* ($k$ a positive integer). Which of I, II,
III, taken individually, is equivalent to $(*)$? (Yes/No triple, rows **A**–**H**.)

- **I** if $k$ is a power of $2$ then $2^{k}+1$ is prime
- **II** $2^{k}+1$ is not prime **only if** $k$ is not a power of $2$
- **III** a **sufficient** condition for $k$ to be a power of $2$ is that $2^{k}+1$ is prime

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer G

[*(Arg1 · statement forms — S1)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G** (No, No, Yes).

Write $(*)$ as $P\Rightarrow Q$ with $P=$ "$2^{k}+1$ prime", $Q=$ "$k$ a power of $2$".

- **I** is $Q\Rightarrow P$ — the **converse**. Not equivalent. **No.**
- **II** "$\lnot P$ only if $\lnot Q$" means $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ — the **inverse**, which is
  equivalent to the converse, **not** to $(*)$. **No.**
- **III** "$P$ is sufficient for $Q$" means $P\Rightarrow Q$ — that is $(*)$ itself. **Yes.**

*The only equivalent restatement is the contrapositive $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ — none of these three is
that, except III which is just $(*)$ reworded with the word "sufficient".*
:::

## Question 12

$\sin x\cos^{2}x=p^{2}\sin x$ has $n$ distinct solutions in $0\leq x\leq2\pi$. Which is/are true? &nbsp;&nbsp;
**I** $n=3$ is **sufficient** for $p>1$ &nbsp; **II** $n=7$ **only if** $-1<p<1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**A** none &nbsp; **B** I &nbsp; **C** II &nbsp; **D** I and II

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer C

[*(Arg2 + trigonometry — S3)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C** (II only).

**Step 1 — Factorise.** $\sin x\cos^{2}x-p^{2}\sin x=\sin x\,(\cos^{2}x-p^{2})=0$, so $\sin x=0$ **or**
$\cos^{2}x=p^{2}$.

**Step 2 — Count.** $\sin x=0$ always gives $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ — **3** solutions. Then $\cos^{2}x=p^{2}$:

- $\lvert p\rvert\geq1$: no new solutions (either impossible, or $\cos x=\pm1$ already counted) $\Rightarrow n=3$;
- $0<\lvert p\rvert<1$: $\cos x=\pm\lvert p\rvert$ gives $4$ new solutions $\Rightarrow n=7$;
- $p=0$: $\cos x=0$ gives $2$ new $\Rightarrow n=5$.

**Step 3 — Judge the statements.**

- **I:** $n=3$ occurs for all $\lvert p\rvert\geq1$ (e.g. $p=-2$ or $p=1$), so it does **not** force $p>1$.
  **False.**
- **II:** $n=7$ occurs exactly when $0<\lvert p\rvert<1$, which lies inside $-1<p<1$. So $n=7\Rightarrow
  -1<p<1$. **True.**
:::

## Question 13

Which **one** statement is a **sufficient** condition for **exactly three** of the other four? &nbsp;&nbsp;
**A** $x\geq0$ &nbsp; **B** $x=1$ &nbsp; **C** $x=0$ or $x=1$ &nbsp; **D** $x\geq0$ or $x\leq1$ &nbsp;
**E** $x\geq0$ and $x\leq1$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer C

[*(Arg2 · sufficient — S3)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** First note **D** ($x\geq0$ or $x\leq1$) is true for *every* real $x$.

Test **C** ($x=0$ or $x=1$) as the hypothesis — does it imply each other statement?

- **A** ($x\geq0$): both $0$ and $1$ are $\geq0$ — **yes**.
- **B** ($x=1$): fails at $x=0$ — **no**.
- **D** (all reals): **yes**.
- **E** ($0\leq x\leq1$): both $0,1$ lie in $[0,1]$ — **yes**.

So **C** implies exactly three others (A, D, E) but not B. *(Checking the rest: A implies only D; B implies
all four; E implies A and D; D implies none — so C is the unique answer.)*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

## Question 14

Lines $ax+by+c=0$, $bx+cy+a=0$, $cx+ay+b=0$ ($a,b,c\neq0$). Which is correct? &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** if two of
the lines are perpendicular, then the third is parallel to $y=x$. *(and other options)*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer F

[*(Arg1 + coordinate geometry — S1)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**F.**

**Step 1 — Write the three gradients.**
$$m_1=-\frac ab,\qquad m_2=-\frac bc,\qquad m_3=-\frac ca.$$

**Step 2 — Their product is fixed.**
$$m_1 m_2 m_3=\left(-\frac ab\right)\left(-\frac bc\right)\left(-\frac ca\right)=-\frac{abc}{abc}=-1.$$

**Step 3 — Use perpendicularity.** If two of the lines are perpendicular, the product of *their* two
gradients is $-1$. Since all three multiply to $-1$, the remaining gradient is $\dfrac{-1}{-1}=1$ — so the
third line has gradient $1$, i.e. is **parallel to $y=x$**.
:::

## Question 15

What is the value of the recurring base-$2$ number $0.\dot0\dot01\dot1=0.001100110011\ldots$? &nbsp;&nbsp;
**A** $\tfrac13$ &nbsp; **B** $\tfrac15$ &nbsp; **C** $\tfrac1{15}$ &nbsp; **D** $\tfrac2{15}$ &nbsp;
**E** $\tfrac4{15}$ &nbsp; **F** $\tfrac3{16}$ &nbsp; **G** $\tfrac5{16}$ &nbsp; **H** $\tfrac6{31}$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer B
**B** ($\tfrac15$).

**Step 1 — Repeating block.** The block "$0011$" repeats, with period $4$. Its value as a binary integer is
$0\cdot2^{3}+0\cdot2^{2}+1\cdot2+1=3$.

**Step 2 — Sum the geometric series.** A block of length $4$ repeating just after the point gives
$$0.\overline{0011}_2=\frac{3}{2^{4}-1}=\frac{3}{15}=\frac15.$$
*(This is the base-$2$ version of the base-$10$ rule "$0.\overline{d_1\ldots d_k}=\dfrac{\text{block}}{10^{k}-1}$".)*
:::

## Question 16

$u_1=a,\ u_2=b,\ u_{n+2}=u_n+u_{n+1}$, with $a,b$ positive integers and $\gcd(a,b)=7$. Which **must** be
true? &nbsp;&nbsp; **I** $u_{2023}$ is a multiple of $7$ &nbsp; **II** if $u_1$ is not a factor of $u_2$
then $u_1$ is not a factor of $u_n$ for any $n>1$ &nbsp; **III** $\gcd(u_1,u_5)=7$ &nbsp;&nbsp; (options
**A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer B
**B** (I only).

**Step 1 — Every term is a multiple of $7$.** Since $\gcd(a,b)=7$, both $a$ and $b$ are multiples of $7$;
and a sum of multiples of $7$ is a multiple of $7$. By the recurrence, all $u_n$ are multiples of $7$. So
**I is true**.

**Step 2 — III fails.** $u_5=2a+3b$, so $\gcd(u_1,u_5)=\gcd(a,2a+3b)=\gcd(a,3b)$. Take $a=21,\,b=7$
($\gcd=7$): then $u_5=63$ and $\gcd(21,63)=21\neq7$. **III false.**

**Step 3 — II fails.** The coefficient of $b$ in $u_4=a+2b$ is $2$. Take $a=14,\,b=7$: $u_1=14$ does **not**
divide $u_2=7$, yet $u_4=14+14=28$ **is** divisible by $14$. **II false.**
:::

## Question 17

$\lceil x\rceil$ is $x$ rounded **up** to the nearest integer. Find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{99}
2^{\lceil x\rceil}\,\mathrm dx$. &nbsp;&nbsp; **A** $2^{99}$ &nbsp; **B** $2^{99}-1$ &nbsp; **C**
$2^{99}-2$ &nbsp; **D** $2^{100}$ &nbsp; **E** $2^{100}-1$ &nbsp; **F** $2^{100}-2$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer F
**F** ($2^{100}-2$).

**Step 1 — The integrand is a step function.** For $x$ in $(n-1,\,n]$, $\lceil x\rceil=n$, so
$2^{\lceil x\rceil}=2^{n}$ on each unit interval $(n-1,n]$, $n=1,2,\dots,99$.

**Step 2 — Add the strips (each width $1$).**
$$\int_{0}^{99}2^{\lceil x\rceil}\,\mathrm dx=\sum_{n=1}^{99}2^{n}\cdot 1=2^{1}+2^{2}+\dots+2^{99}
=2^{100}-2,$$
using $2+2^{2}+\dots+2^{99}=2\!\left(2^{99}-1\right)=2^{100}-2$.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,3.0))
for n in range(1,6):
    plt.plot([n-1,n],[2**n,2**n],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
    plt.plot([n,n],[2**n,2**(n+1)],color='#2b6cb0',lw=0.6,ls=':')
plt.xticks(range(0,6)); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('2^⌈x⌉')
plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.title('2^⌈x⌉ is constant 2ⁿ on each interval (n−1, n]')
plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 18

$x^{4}+bx^{2}+c=0$ has four distinct real roots **if and only if** which condition? &nbsp;&nbsp;
**A** $b^{2}>4c$ &nbsp; **B** $b^{2}<4c$ &nbsp; **C** $c>0$ and $b>2\sqrt c$ &nbsp; **D** $c>0$ and
$b<-2\sqrt c$ &nbsp; **E** $c<0$ and $b<0$ &nbsp; **F** $c<0$ and $b>0$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer D
**D.**

**Step 1 — Substitute $u=x^{2}$.** The equation becomes $u^{2}+bu+c=0$. Four distinct real $x$ need **two
distinct positive** roots $u$ (each positive $u$ gives $x=\pm\sqrt u$).

**Step 2 — Conditions for two distinct positive roots.**
$$\text{distinct real: } b^{2}-4c>0;\qquad \text{sum } -b>0\ (b<0);\qquad \text{product } c>0.$$

**Step 3 — Combine.** With $c>0$, "$b<0$ and $b^{2}>4c$" is exactly $b<-2\sqrt c$. So the condition is
**$c>0$ and $b<-2\sqrt c$**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-2.4,2.4,400)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,3.2))
plt.plot(x,x**4-5*x**2+4,color='#2b6cb0')   # b=-5,c=4: b<-2√4=-4, c>0
for r in [-2,-1,1,2]: plt.plot(r,0,'o',color='crimson')
plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.7); plt.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.title('b=−5, c=4 (b<−2√c): four distinct real roots ±1, ±2')
plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 19

$f$ is a non-constant polynomial and $g(x)=x\,f''(x)$; $f=0$ for exactly $M$ real $x$, $g=0$ for exactly
$N$ real $x$. Which are possible? &nbsp;&nbsp; **I** $M<N$ &nbsp; **II** $M=N$ &nbsp; **III** $M>N$
&nbsp;&nbsp; (options **A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer H
**H** (all three). $g=0$ means $x=0$ **or** $f''(x)=0$; give one example of each case.

- **$M<N$:** $f(x)=x^{4}+1$ has $M=0$ real roots; $f''=12x^{2}$, so $g=12x^{3}$ has the single root $x=0$,
  giving $N=1$. Here $0<1$.
- **$M=N$:** $f(x)=x^{2}$ has $M=1$ ($x=0$); $f''=2\neq0$, so $g=2x$ has $N=1$.
- **$M>N$:** $f(x)=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$ has $M=4$ (roots $\pm1,\pm2$); $f''=12x^{2}-10$, so
  $g=x(12x^{2}-10)$ has roots $0,\pm\sqrt{10/12}$, giving $N=3$. Here $4>3$.

All three orderings occur, so **H**.
:::

## Question 20

$f$ a real polynomial; for $p<q$, $\displaystyle I_{p,q}=\int_{p}^{q}\Big[(f(x))^{2}-(f(\lvert
x\rvert))^{2}\Big]\mathrm dx$. Which **must** be true? &nbsp;&nbsp; **1** $I_{p,q}=0$ only if $0<p$ &nbsp;
**2** $f'(x)<0$ for all $x$ only if $I_{p,q}<0$ for all $p<q<0$ &nbsp; **3** $I_{p,q}>0$ only if $p<0$
&nbsp;&nbsp; (options **A** none … **H** all)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution — Answer D
**D** (3 only).

**Step 1 — The integrand vanishes for $x\geq0$.** When $x\geq0$, $\lvert x\rvert=x$, so
$(f(x))^{2}-(f(\lvert x\rvert))^{2}=0$. Only the part of $[p,q]$ with $x<0$ (where $f(\lvert
x\rvert)=f(-x)$) can contribute.

**Step 2 — Statement 3 is TRUE.** If $p\geq0$ the whole interval is in $x\geq0$, so $I_{p,q}=0$; thus
$I_{p,q}>0$ is impossible unless $p<0$. So $I_{p,q}>0\Rightarrow p<0$. ✓

**Step 3 — Statements 1 and 2 fail.**

- **1:** if $f$ is **even** then $f(x)=f(-x)$, the integrand is $0$ everywhere and $I_{p,q}=0$ even with
  $p<0$ — so "$I_{p,q}=0$ only if $0<p$" is false.
- **2:** take $f(x)=-x$ (so $f'=-1<0$ for all $x$). Then $(f(x))^{2}=x^{2}=(f(-x))^{2}$, the integrand is
  $0$, and $I_{p,q}=0$, not $<0$. So the implication fails.
:::
